observation.visible_scene: An elevated/aerial view of a wide waterfall with emerald-green plunging water. Upstream, a broad river churns into white rapids toward the brink, with a few low rocky islets and a small cluster of dark rocks protruding at the lip. In the far background a long bridge spans the water against a tree-lined, overcast shoreline. The lower part of the frame shows the falling sheets of water and, increasingly, a white mist plume rising from the base.
visible_changes: The water is in continuous turbulent motion throughout: the white foam band along the brink churns, breaks, and reforms frame-to-frame, and the surface ripples of the upstream river keep shifting toward the edge.

The vertical green sheets of falling water keep cascading over the lip; their texture and the boundary between foam and clear water change constantly, indicating steady flow rather than a single event.
A white mist cloud at the bottom of the frame becomes progressively larger and more prominent from early to late frames, partially obscuring the lower part of the falling water.

The whole scene content shifts slightly upward across the clip (the brink moves from roughly the lower-middle toward the middle of the frame), consistent with a slow camera reframe (mild tilt-down / pull-back) that reveals more of the plunge and the base mist.

Background landmarks—the bridge, the tree line, the rocky islets, and the dark rocks at the brink—remain essentially fixed in position relative to one another, confirming the geography is static while only the water and the framing change.
outside_clip_unknowns: The full height of the fall and the plunge pool below the mist are not shown.
What drives the flow (upstream conditions, time of day changes) and any events before or after this segment are unseen.
Whether the growing mist is an actual increase in spray or simply more of it entering the frame due to the camera reframe cannot be resolved from these frames alone.
uncertain_details: Exact camera motion (tilt-down vs. zoom-out vs. slow drone drift) is ambiguous; the background barely moves, so only a small net upward shift of the scene is supported.
Individual water features cannot be tracked as discrete objects; the described changes are pattern evolution of turbulent flow, not translation of a specific parcel.
The apparent thickening of the foam at the crest may be natural flow variation rather than a directional change.
